newsitem.title: UK: Esso UK stations see red in Tiger Tokens.
newsitem.headline: Esso UK stations see red in Tiger Tokens.

text.p: Some U.K. petrol stations selling the Esso brand claim the U.S.-based oil giant is demanding nearly 50 million sterling in charges tied to the defunct Tiger Token promotional scheme that ended in 1996 after a 10-year run.

Motorists were given one token for every six pounds spent at an Esso station which in turn could be redeemed for gifts. Esso is the U.K. market leader with an estimated 1,980 sites, down from 2,028 in 1995, according to industry data.

The Esso Licensed Retailers Association (ELRA), representing some 600 stations, said the cost to each licensee for participating in the program was increased at the same time the company was launching its Pricewatch campaign early last year.

"The amount of money that licensees are expected to pay is on top of these site rental increases and lowering fuel margins that have been to pay for Pricewatch...the licensees do not have the ability to meet all the bills," said Paul Horan, spokesman for ELRA, adding there was no written contract outlining costs for Tiger Tokens.
The licensees are being asked to pay for additional costs even though Esso lost market share to the supermarkets during that time, he said.
"Bear in mind that a promotion by one of the largest companies in the world failed," he said.

A unit of Exxon Corp, Esso's Pricewatch promised to match its lowest-priced competitors in the U.K. in a bid to regain market share after the supermarkets began undercutting most of its rivals. The cut-throat price competition led to a near 10 percent reduction in the number of filling stations last year.
An Esso spokeswoman told Reuters the outstanding debt was "substantially less" than 50 million sterling and that many retailers have either paid or are making payments.

"Clearly there will be a continuing period of time where those payments are coming in," the spokeswoman said. "The liabilities associated with this promotion were known throughout the length of the promotion."
ELRA's allegations come on top of a complaint filed with the European Commission earlier this year demanding Esso provide "commercial and financial benefits" in their licensee agreements.
The group, which plans to meet German and Dutch licensees in Brussels on June 11, claims Esso raised the rent and cut the margins provided to station owners in order to pay for Pricewatch.

"The other complaint (from ELRA) is that Esso claims to have gotten back their market share but there has been no reduction in fees and has been an increase," in January, Horan said. "They're still paying for a price war that has ceased."
Esso said there were no plans to change its licensee agreements based on Pricewatch and that it expected the EC to find that the company has acted legally in those agreements.
